title: Shot- and Noise-Aware Pauli Correlation Encoding for Max-Cut Experiments on IBM Heron Quantum Processor
abstract: Pauli correlation encoding (PCE) encodes $m$ binary variables in the signs of $k$-body Pauli correlators of $n=O(m^{1/k})$ qubits, and trains a parameterized circuit on a relaxed loss of sharpness $α$. The strongest published schedules sharpen this loss aggressively and are benchmarked with exact expectation values, whereas a quantum computer estimates correlators from a finite number of shots. We show that the sharpness is a hidden shot budget. Since the expected sign of a correlator estimated from $S$ shots, $\mathrm{erf}(c\sqrt{S/2})$, agrees with $\tanh(0.851\sqrt{S}\,c)$ to within $0.019$, the edge term of the relaxed loss at $α=0.851\sqrt{S}$ approximately equals, up to a constant, minus twice the cut expected from decoding $S$ shots. This explains why schedules tuned with exact expectation values lose their advantage at realistic budgets, and yields a shot-aware schedule whose final sharpness is set by the shot budget. On five G-set graphs with $800$ variables on $13$ qubits, this schedule outperforms every published schedule at its target budget in all $150$ paired comparisons of the decoded circuit output, owing to the sharpness at $1.6\times10^4$ shots and mostly to switching off the regularization at $10^3$; after a classical bit-swap search, it remains the best on average at $1.6\times10^4$ shots. Device noise damps the correlators by a factor $s$, which amounts to a smaller shot budget $s^2S$. On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, an all-to-all ansatz of the type used for the best published G-set results compiles to $835$ CZ gates and decodes to a random cut, while our $96$-CZ hardware-native circuit, trained in simulation and sharpened to $α\simeq0.65\,s\sqrt{S}$, retains up to $0.919$ of the best-known cut. For new circuits, a damping and an offset calibrated on other circuits of the same graph predicted the decoded cuts at $10^3$ shots to within $0.002$.
summary: This work tackles the Max-Cut problem using Pauli Correlation Encoding on quantum processors. The authors introduce a crucial 'shot-aware' training schedule that correctly links the required optimization sharpness to the actual number of measurement shots available. This methodology significantly improves performance on real hardware by accurately accounting for measurement noise and finite sampling.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of solving NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, specifically Max-Cut, using quantum computation.
main_result: A novel shot-aware training schedule is proposed that accounts for finite measurement budgets and device noise, leading to superior performance compared to previous methods on both simulated and physical quantum hardware.
method: It employs Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) to map binary variables to Pauli correlators, optimizing a relaxed loss function using a schedule whose sharpness is determined by the available shot budget ($S$).
model_or_system: The problem is framed as finding the ground state of a classical Ising model (Max-Cut). The implementation is tested on the IBM Heron quantum processor, utilizing hardware-native ansatz circuits.
key_observables: Approximation ratio ($r(\mathbf{x})$), measured Pauli correlators, and the final decoded cut weight.
important_parameters: Shot budget ($S$), sharpness parameter ($\alpha$), and device noise damping factor ($s$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the required training sharpness ($\alpha$) scales predictably with the shot budget ($\alpha \propto \sqrt{S}$), correcting previous overestimations based on exact expectation values.
figures_summary: The notes reference tables comparing approximation ratios across various schedules and shot counts, and tables detailing the damping of measured correlators on the physical device.
paper_structure: The paper develops from the theoretical equivalence of Max-Cut to an Ising model, introduces the PCE and the relaxed loss function, derives the shot-aware scheduling principle, and concludes with extensive comparative results on both simulation and the IBM Heron hardware.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, hardware-aware methodology for improving variational quantum algorithms by correctly modeling the impact of finite measurement resources (shots) and device noise on optimization schedules.

The classical computer (CPU) estimates the m correlators from the recorded bit strings, evaluates the relaxed loss of Eq. (7), and updates the circuit parameters. After training, the spins are decoded from the signs of the measured correlators, and the cut of Eq. (1) is evaluated classically.
